newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Europeans strive to reach maximum gas oil output.
newsitem.headline: Europeans strive to reach maximum gas oil output.

text.p: European refineries that have lagged behind their U.S. counterparts in flexibility have made greater strides than normal in reaching maximum gas oil output this autumn.

Middle distillate output in the European Union rose 1.2 percent in October despite a drop of 1.0 percent in total net output and a fall of 2.7 percent in crude intake, according to Euroilstock figures released last Friday. The figures exclude Sweden.

In the United States a greater degree of marginal cracking capacity allows refiners to substitute gasoline for gas oil. In Europe, refiners have generally had to push more crude in to maximise any one product.

"In Europe, the marginal distillate source has tended to be straight-running..., (so) it is quite a surprise to see the capacity utilisation down, but the production (of middle distillates) up," said UBS energy economist Geoff Pyne.
Already in September, some analysts said distillate output had reached a peak.
But a greater sweet crude slate, and perhaps some ingenuity, has tweaked a little more distillate out of the pipes.
"I have been a bit surprised. Now it looks like they're really testing the system and being as creative as possible," said Cindy Poynter of oil analysts Bonner and Moore.

The incentive has clearly been there. In volume terms, in which the end-user prices are calculated, heating oil barges in the ARA market have been consistently more expensive than eurograde gasoline since mid-August. This month, heating oil prices have generally been higher by 15-20 percent.
"We haven't seen such a strong gas oil market since late 1993," Poynter said.
This year, distillate hydrocracking capacity has actually fallen 3,560 barrels per day (bpd), says Wood Mackenzie.

Mild hydrocracking is up 97,000 bpd, but the units built or upgraded are designed to remove sulphur and metals from the feedstock. They improve the quality of the gas oil, but are no help in raising the quantity.

Next year, however, refinery upgrading means that European majors will be more flexible and require much less tweaking. Analysts say it is a sign of the growing maturity of the European refining stock.

"It used to be that Europe was lagging. Now it seems to be catching up (with the U.S.). Over the next six months, we will see considerable expansion...bringing in a lot of new hydrocracking," said Peter Bogin, associate director at Cambridge Energy Research Associates in Paris.
Very soon, a hydrocracker and CCR unit at Tupras's Izmit refinery is due to open. The $377 million Turkish hydrocracker project will be finished some 10 weeks ahead of schedule.
Shell in the Netherlands is to complete its Perplus project, including at hydrocracking unit, by the end of May.
Hydrocracking capacity at BP's Grangemouth refinery in the U.K. will also expand from 35,000 to 40,000 bpd by the second quarter next year.
In the second half of 1997, AGIP expects a new 20,000 bpd hydrocracker will be on stream at its Milazzo refinery.
"Certainly, we will have to go back to the drawing board to see what the maximum distillate capacity is," said Peter Bogin
